payload.title: What Are the Japanese Wedding Traditions You Did Not Know?
protect_keywords: 5 charming japanese wedding traditions (old URL; SEO to quantify US and AU)
payload.audience: Couples in their 30s interested in destination weddings and luxury experiences, AUD 150k+ budget
payload.reader: An Australian couple in their 30s with a generous budget, often with a Japanese partner or parents, who want to understand what the families will expect (yuinō, a Shinto or chapel ceremony, san-san-kudo, shiromuku and iro-uchikake, the hirōen, goshūgi, the bride's letter), honour the customs respectfully, and decide whether to marry in Japan (Smartraveller: exercise normal safety precautions overall, reconsider travel only to the Fukushima Dai-ichi restricted areas) or bring the customs into a wedding at home.
payload.goal: Read the free Wedded Wonderland digital magazine (primary CTA); secondary, in-context invitation to speak with a Wedded Advisor placed after the 'for Australians' section.
payload.angle: Most lists reduce a Japanese wedding to a sake toast and a kimono. We walk through it in wedding order as families live it: yuinō between the families, the Shinto ceremony before the kami with san-san-kudo, the shiromuku and the change into iro-uchikake, the chapel ceremony many couples choose, then the hirōen with goshūgi, hikidemono, kagami biraki, speeches and the bride's letter to her parents. Garment names and meanings follow Japan's museums, shrine bodies and JNTO; everything else is living practice that varies by family and region. We close with what Australians need, as Smartraveller and the Australian Embassy in Tokyo word it, and how couples bring these customs into a wedding at home.
must_include: One early framing line: customs vary by family and region, and between Shinto, chapel and civil-only weddings

About 11 to 12 numbered sections in wedding order: yuinō, Shinto ceremony, san-san-kudo, bridal dress, chapel weddings, hirōen and oiro-naoshi, goshūgi and hikidemono, kagami biraki, speeches and the bride's letter, senbazuru, UNESCO, for Australians
Japanese terms with macrons as sources give them (yuinō, hirōen, goshūgi); inline definitions
Goshūgi and hikidemono described with no amounts or price ranges
UNESCO washoku (2013) quoted only as far as its own text links to celebrations or weddings, if confirmed live

Section for Australians: Smartraveller overall level and the Fukushima Dai-ichi restricted areas, update date (as at November 2026), heat and typhoon seasons, entry line, Australian Embassy Tokyo and Consulate-General Osaka for CNI or affidavit and notarial, 'Getting married overseas', municipal office registration or questions to ask including any fees; Kyoto, Tokyo, Hakone as places couples choose; Japanese-Australian weddings at home
FAQ of 5 to 7 questions with no amounts, covering the old page's query coverage (san san kudo, kimono, gifts)
Internal links: /destinations/asia; Chinese and Indonesian traditions drafts where natural; /expert-advice/wedding-traditions pillar

tradition_plan.note: Planner (wedding-planner-sme) runs batch A and batch B in parallel, scratch folders 02-research/batch-a and 02-research/batch-b, 15 min HARD by the clock, save after every 3 facts, no extra sourcing rounds, never retry a declined call. Preferred sources: japan.travel (JNTO), Jinja Honcho and shrine pages, Kokugakuin Encyclopedia of Shinto, Tokyo National Museum, Kyoto Costume Institute, V&A, UNESCO, Britannica, academic sources. Never competitor wedding sites, vendor blogs or Wikipedia. Unsourced customs are written as living practice with no meaning or origin as fact and no [[VERIFY]] marker; 'often told' at most once per post. Source gaps go in the run report only (authority rule).
